OVERSIGHT OF THE FEDERAL ENERGY 
REGULATORY COMMISSION 
WEDNESDAY, JULY 22, 2026 
U.S. SENATE, 
COMMITTEE ON ENERGY AND NATURAL RESOURCES, 
Washington, DC. 
The Committee met, pursuant to notice, at 9:33 a.m. in Room 
SD–366, Dirksen Senate Office Building, Hon. Mike Lee, Chairman 
of the Committee, presiding. 
OPENING STATEMENT OF HON. MIKE LEE, 
U.S. SENATOR FROM UTAH 
The CHAIRMAN. The Committee will come to order. I apologize for 
the late start time. I serve on the Foreign Relations Committee, 
along with a couple of our members, and as we often find ourselves 
in that position, we were in a markup, and had any of us left, they 
would have lost a quorum. So, we ran over here as quickly as we 
could. 
Today, the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources holds a 
hearing to conduct oversight over the Federal Energy Regulatory 
Commission (FERC). Pursuant to the Federal Power Act and the 
Natural Gas Act, the Commission regulates the interstate trans-
mission and wholesale market of electricity and natural gas, as 
well as oil and gas pipelines and hydroelectric power. It ensures 
that electricity rates are just and reasonable, and licenses facilities 
within its statutory jurisdiction. All of these things happen to be 
vital to America’s energy dominance, ensuring both our security 
and prosperity at home and also our ability to advance the inter-
ests of the United States on the world stage by supplying the en-
ergy needs of others. 
Today, we will be hearing from FERC’s five Commissioners to re-
port on their priorities and the Commission’s operations. They are 
Chairman Laura Swett, and Commissioners David Rosner, Lindsay 
See, Judy Chang, and David LaCerte. Following my opening state-
ment today and that of Ranking Member Heinrich, we will hear 
opening statements from each of the Commissioners, followed by 
questions from each of the Senators in attendance. 
There was a time when the Federal Energy Regulatory Commis-
sion operated largely outside the public spotlight. Those days, of 
course, are now over. FERC now sits at the center of some of the 
most important questions facing our country—reliable electricity, 
affordable energy, data centers, manufacturing, and national secu-
rity. Every one of these issues, in its own way, now runs directly 
through FERC. Some estimates suggest that the Commission regu-

2 
lates activity representing roughly five percent of the American 
economy. This, of course, understates the matter because, in re-
ality, the Commission’s influence reaches much, much further than 
that. Energy is an input for basically everything we produce, every-
thing we do. So, when energy becomes more expensive, or when it 
becomes less reliable, every American pays the price in far more 
ways than one. 
That, of course, makes FERC’s mission more important now than 
ever. The United States is experiencing the fastest growth in elec-
tricity demand in a generation. After years of relatively flat load 
growth, utilities across our country are now forecasting dramatic 
increases—increases driven by data centers, artificial intelligence, 
advanced manufacturing, electrification, and industrial develop-
ment. It means America is building again. It means investment is 
returning, but none of it happens if we cannot produce and deliver 
enough reliable electricity. 
That’s why I was encouraged by the Commission’s recent action 
under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act addressing how re-
gional transmission organizations and independent system opera-
tors manage large-load interconnections. Rather than imposing a 
rigid one-size-fits-all federal mandate, the Commission directed six 
regional grid operators to reexamine how large data centers and 
other major new customers might connect to the grid, with par-
ticular attention to interconnection delays, who pays for the nec-
essary upgrades, and what impact all these things might ulti-
mately have on consumers. 
These are extraordinarily difficult questions. No one suggests 
that they are easy. Large data centers create tremendous economic 
opportunity, but they also consume enormous amounts of elec-
tricity. Existing ratepayers should not be forced to subsidize costs 
that properly belong to new entrants. But we also cannot allow out-
dated processes to prevent new investment from connecting to the 
grid. Getting that balance right will of course be difficult, but I am 
confident that if you maintain your current trajectory, you, as our 
Commissioners, will be more than up to that great task. 
I am also encouraged by FERC’s recent efforts to improve the 
permitting process for natural gas infrastructure. FERC is modern-
izing environmental reviews, reducing unnecessary delays—those 
that don’t provide any additional value added on the environmental 
front—and it’s expanding the use of blanket certificates for routine 
upgrades. Every year that we happen to delay needed infrastruc-
ture is another year that Americans have to pay higher prices and 
face greater reliability risks. 
More importantly, I hope today’s discussion reinforces something 
that should unite all of us, regardless of political party. As this 
Committee continues its work on permitting reform, I hope we can 
build on the bipartisan momentum that has emerged around many 
of these issues. I look forward to getting perspectives from each one 
of you today on the challenges ahead and to working with each of 
you to ensure that we lower costs for consumers while simulta-
neously improving grid reliability. 
Ranking Member Heinrich.

3 
OPENING STATEMENT OF HON. MARTIN HEINRICH, 
U.S. SENATOR FROM NEW MEXICO 
Senator HEINRICH. Thank you, Chairman Lee, and special 
thanks to all five of FERC’s Commissioners for attending this hear-
ing today. We very much appreciate having you here. 
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has long been an 
important independent agency. It serves the public interest by reg-
ulating electricity, hydroelectric dams, natural gas, and oil in a 
manner that is both fair and impartial from the President and from 
Congress, as required by statute. Now, historically considered by 
some to be a bit of a sleepy agency, FERC faces a very pivotal time 
in our nation’s history right now. Electricity prices are rising, and 
electricity supply has not been able to keep up with demand. Ac-
cording to a recent report, 75 percent of U.S. adults say that they 
have noticed their home energy costs increasing in recent years. 
Some of that blame can be squarely placed on our current Presi-
dent. I recently released a report on how this administration is 
waging a war on cheap, clean energy, and the impact of that is ris-
ing energy costs. The administration is slow-walking installing 73 
gigawatts—think about that, gigawatts—of solar, 43 gigawatts of 
storage, 30 gigawatts of onshore wind, and 16 gigawatts of offshore 
wind. Constraining this buildout would increase economy-wide util-
ity costs by approximately $11.6 billion per year. But that is not 
the only reason that costs are rising. 
We are also seeing a rapid increase in electricity demand and are 
hampered by not getting enough power from generators to end- 
users and struggling to quickly add new needed generation sources. 
Luckily, we can take steps to improve our grid to help move elec-
tricity more efficiently and bring new power sources online. I re-
cently launched an initiative called Grid for Growth, a plan to meet 
surging electricity demand without shifting the costs of that to con-
sumers. This effort complements ongoing efforts to pass bipartisan 
permitting reform. And as part of the effort, last week, I introduced 
the Grid Connection and Congestion Management Act to create a 
faster path for generator interconnection. Modeled after ERCOT’s 
connect-and-manage process, projects are rewarded for being flexi-
ble in their output by getting onto the grid faster. 
Other bills will follow in the next few weeks and months, but our 
ability to meet the rising needs of the grid are based in large part 
on our ability to build more interregional transmission lines. That 
is why permitting reform is so important. Interregional trans-
mission lines can be the best line of defense against extreme 
weather conditions, improving reliability, and reducing consumer 
costs. While FERC requires some interregional transmission plan-
ning under Orders 1000 and 1920, this coordination has not, unfor-
tunately, produced a substantial number of interregional trans-
mission projects in the last decade. We need to find a way to build 
more high-voltage transmission lines in the next decade. Our abil-
ity to grow our economy depends on it. And to FERC’s credit, the 
agency has taken active steps to confront energy challenges. Last 
month, FERC issued six show cause orders, requiring grid opera-
tors and their transmission owners to justify or propose changes to 
their current tariffs with respect to large-load customers. These 
steps by FERC can help protect consumers and encourage grid op-

4 
erators to integrate new advanced technologies when adding new 
large loads to the grid. 
FERC choosing to address major electricity users, like data cen-
ters and manufacturers, is an important step in the right direction. 
Nevertheless, more action can and should be taken to ensure that 
consumers are protected from sky-high costs associated with data 
centers, manufacturers, and other large loads. I have been working 
on a bill intended to do just that and hope to speak more about 
that soon. However, all of these efforts that I mentioned will be 
meaningless if the independence of FERC is erased. The Supreme 
Court’s recent decision has put the impartiality of independent 
agencies at risk. Now, more than ever, FERC’s mission to ensure 
that utility rates remain just and reasonable and not unduly dis-
criminatory or preferential is critical to making sure millions of 
Americans can keep their lights on. During this once-in-a-genera-
tion moment, I continue to believe that regulatory certainty and 
the freedom for commissioners of independent agencies like FERC 
to act in a way to provide that certainty will be critical in meeting 
the energy challenges of today. I hope to discuss these issues with 
each of you during this hearing and very much look forward to it. 
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 
The CHAIRMAN. Thank you, Senator Heinrich. We will now turn 
to each of the Commissioners here today to give their opening 
statements, and of course, your written statements will be entered 
into the record in full. We will begin with the FERC Chairman, 
Laura Swett. The Senate confirmed Chairman Swett back in Octo-
ber of 2025. Prior to that, she served at FERC as a legal advisor 
to two Commissioners, including a former FERC Chairman, and 
she litigated Federal Power Act and Natural Gas Act matters for 
15 years. 
Chairman Swett, you are now recognized, and you may give your 
opening statement. 
OPENING STATEMENT OF HON. LAURA SWETT, CHAIRMAN, 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
Ms. SWETT. Good morning. Thank you, Chairman Lee, Ranking 
Member Heinrich, and members of the Committee for the oppor-
tunity to testify today. My testimony is rooted in the core principles 
that anchor my approach as FERC Chairman: affordability, effi-
ciency, and legal durability. 
For many households, higher utility bills are debilitating burdens 
with personal consequences. I understand this firsthand from my 
childhood. Monthly bills caused me deep anxiety when I was a 
child, and I carry the weight of that financial stress with me every 
day in the way that I lead this agency, and it informs my resolve 
to ensure that families across the country don’t have that same 
burden in shouldering unnecessary costs. As electricity demand ac-
celerates, the Commission is acting decisively to ensure that the 
grid remains reliable and affordable. For too long, this country has 
deferred critical decisions essential to maintaining the grid, and 
that era has ended. The responsibility to steer our country through 
the energy future is squarely upon me and my four colleagues. The 
Commission’s actions under my leadership reflect an unwavering

5 
commitment to our statutory obligations to ensure just and reason-
able rates. 
At no point in its history has FERC advanced a more comprehen-
sive set of reforms designed to safeguard American consumers—nor 
been, I think, subject to leadership as consumed with honoring the 
law as I am. 
From aggressively modernizing natural gas permitting to insti-
tuting far-reaching transparency requirements in our June orders, 
we are executing a disciplined strategy to reduce costs while rein-
forcing reliability and encouraging infrastructure investment, and 
that is a very tough needle to thread, and I am committed to doing 
it. At our June meeting, we took bold action to strengthen cost dis-
cipline and reliability. You have mentioned, both of you, that we 
ordered the six jurisdictional electric markets to produce the most 
detailed cost transparency measures the Commission has ever re-
quired. Those actions should equip our state counterparts, who are 
responsible for doling out household bills, with tools to assess the 
expenditures, defend ratepayers, and ensure that emerging load 
drivers, such as data centers, do not impose unjustified costs on 
households or small businesses. Additionally, we have established 
transparent, protective rules for integrating new loads quickly, 
without compromising reliability. 
Still in the vein of affordability, one of the most effective ways 
to lower energy prices is to eliminate infrastructure constraints 
that artificially restrict supply. Recent extreme weather events 
show this clearly. The regions that don’t have enough gas pipeline 
capacity experienced prices many times higher than those with suf-
ficient infrastructure. These disparities translate directly into con-
sumer hardship. In response, the Commission is implementing tar-
geted reforms to streamline permitting and accelerate project de-
velopment. Following the Seven County decision, and under my 
leadership, we are realigning our environmental review practices 
with the Commission’s statutory role as an economic regulator, a 
fact that appears to have been lost on several of my predecessors. 
Since I joined the Commission late last year, FERC has proposed 
significantly expanding blanket authorizations for routine pipeline 
activities and initiated parallel efforts for LNG and hydropower to 
ensure that these projects can move quickly, without burdensome, 
case-specific reviews, but based on FERC’s decades of experience. 
These reforms and deliberate recalibration of our processes will re-
duce administrative friction while preserving full statutory compli-
ance. More energy means lower bills. We are moving fast, but 
maintaining regulatory excellence so that those investing in and 
building infrastructure are less vulnerable to judicial review 
through excellent orders and the associated gridlock and wasted re-
sources that come with orders that are not. 
In closing, the work ahead demands clarity, urgency, and strong 
leadership. Our systems are changing faster than ever, and the 
choices we make now will determine whether the nation is pre-
pared for the coming decades. 
We have taken meaningful steps in the past nine months of my 
tenure, but the path forward requires sustained resolve, smarter 
tools, and dexterity, as new technology and pressures emerge. My 
family and I have made many sacrifices so that I could realize the

6 
honor bestowed upon me by the President to guide our country 
through the next few years and to success on the other side. I take 
that commitment with grave resolve, and so long as I am in charge, 
I will push our country toward an energy system that is affordable, 
resilient, and built for the future, with focus and determination, 
and an unwavering commitment to the American ratepayers, who 
depend on us every single day. 
Thank you.

The CHAIRMAN. Thank you, Chairman Swett. 
We will now hear from Commissioner David Rosner. He formerly 
served as an energy analyst at FERC. He was also someone who 
spent two years detailed to this Committee, in addition to prior 
service that he had at the U.S. Department of Energy. He has 
served on FERC as a Commissioner since 2024, including as Chair-
man for several months in 2025. 
The Chair now recognizes Commissioner David Rosner. 
OPENING STATEMENT OF HON. DAVID ROSNER, COMMIS-
SIONER, FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
Mr. ROSNER. Chairman Lee, Ranking Member Heinrich, and 
members of the Committee, it is an honor to appear before you 
alongside my colleagues to discuss FERC’s work to deliver afford-
able and reliable energy for all Americans and our commitment to 
upholding Congress’s vision for a bipartisan, independent, resource- 
neutral regulator. This mission entrusted to us, while simple to ar-
ticulate, is increasingly complex to execute. Energy demand con-
tinues to grow at a pace that we have not seen in a generation, 
driven by growth in new industries, like artificial intelligence, re-
shoring manufacturing, and increased use of electricity in homes 
and businesses. And we face these challenges at a time when fami-
lies and small businesses struggle with high prices, especially in 
their utility bills. So, while meeting this moment presents chal-
lenges, it also creates opportunities for us to modernize our nation’s 
energy infrastructure. Upgrading our energy system is necessary to 
ensure that every American receives reliable and affordable power, 
and it is essential to our country’s economic competitiveness and 
national security. With this in mind, I would like to highlight a few 
of the specific actions FERC has taken to confront the challenges 
and realize the opportunities before us. 
First, we are accelerating the addition of new electric generation 
of all kinds. Building the energy resources needed to meet growing 
demand and reducing consumer costs is my top focus. We have im-
plemented FERC’s landmark Order No. 2023 generator inter-
connection reforms and fast-tracked more than 50 gigawatts of 
shovel-ready power plants. Looking forward, I am encouraging grid 
operators to deploy automation and artificial intelligence tools that 
have been shown to accelerate steps in the interconnection study 
process from years to weeks. 
Second, we are establishing forward-looking grid planning, cen-
tered around reliability, affordability, and economic growth. This 
year, FERC will begin acting on transmission providers’ proposals 
to implement Order No. 1920, which modernized long-term trans-
mission planning. When I arrived as a Commissioner, this rule was 
divided along party lines. Today, thanks to extensive state engage-
ment and collaborative problem-solving, I am very proud that it is 
bipartisan and unanimously supported. 
Third, we are emphasizing predictability, speed, and legal dura-
bility for infrastructure permitting. Since January 2025, FERC has 
issued over 120 permits for hydropower and natural gas projects, 
moving from NEPA review to final permit more than 30 percent 
faster than was typical during the last decade. Critically, we have 
done this without compromising quality. FERC’s permits have been

10 
routinely upheld in court in recent years. And looking to the future, 
permitting efficiency will become only more essential as demand 
growth accelerates. 
Fourth, we are embracing innovative pathways to power data 
centers and other large loads while protecting consumers. Over the 
last year, the Commission has acted to ensure that demand growth 
leads to a more reliable, affordable, and sustainable grid and that 
America can win the AI race without regular families paying for it. 
At FERC, this is another top priority. In December and January, 
the Commission implemented programs in the PJM and SPP re-
gions to pair new large loads with new generation. This pairing re-
duces how much these projects lean on the grid, it minimizes the 
need to construct additional transmission upgrades, it promotes 
flexible operations, and it helps ensure that new loads pay their 
fair share. In parallel, more than 30 states have adopted special re-
tail rate structures for large loads, an important complement to 
FERC action and a reminder of the cooperative federalism needed 
to protect regular consumers. 
Finally, building upon the progress and the record developed in 
response to Secretary Wright’s ANOPR, in June the Commission 
issued a show cause order to each regional grid operator, asking 
them to modernize their rules for interconnecting large loads. 
These orders are based upon four key pillars—protect consumers, 
enhance transparency, safeguard reliability, and foster innovation. 
Put simply, the goal is lowering costs, protecting grid reliability, 
and helping new customers and power plants get online faster. 
Fifth, we continue to enhance grid security and reliability 
through modernization and flexibility. It is essential that we con-
tinue to deploy 21st-century reliability solutions, like advanced de-
mand response, dynamic line ratings, predictive artificial intel-
ligence, and emerging cybersecurity technologies. And FERC’s work 
now includes the development of robust reliability standards for 
large loads. 
Sixth, we are staying laser-focused on affordability. In addition 
to the examples I have already mentioned, over the last two years, 
FERC has approved expanded competitive electric markets in the 
West and in the Southeast, which will enable customers access to 
lower-cost power. And in PJM, we approved a temporary price cap 
that saved consumers more than $25 billion. It is my priority to de-
liver more examples like this in 2026. 
Finally, I will conclude by highlighting the value of our current 
consensus-driven mindset. I am immensely proud that the vast ma-
jority of orders I have voted on have been bipartisan and unani-
mous, including every single energy project permit. This consensus 
ensures regulatory predictability, legal durability, and strong out-
comes for all Americans, informed by five distinct perspectives 
among the Commissioners. I want to thank my colleagues for their 
collaboration, which I am confident will continue to deliver for our 
country. Thank you again for the opportunity to testify today, and 
I look forward to your questions.

Question 1: DOE recently issued its draft National Transmission Needs Study, which found

Answer: The buildout of high-voltage interregional transmission is essential to maintaining the

evaluate potential projects with a common set of benefits, one of which specifically examines the

Question 2: FERC has made improvements to generator interconnection processes through

high network upgrades?

Question 2: Under its five categories of reform for the June 2026 show cause orders, FERC
includes "preventing cost shifting and requiring transparency into transmission costs." How will
FERC ensure that large loads, including data centers, bear their fair share of grid modernization
costs and do not shift those costs onto residential ratepayers, particularly given states' central
role in regulating cost-shifting?
Answer: My colleagues and I take seriously concerns about protecting residential ratepayers
from the costs of integrating large loads, including data centers, and these concerns factored
heavily in the Commission's historic show cause orders. The orders the Commission issued in
June 2026 establish rigorous consumer safeguards. For example, the orders focus on preventing
